Chapter 6: The Pull of Europe and the Lessons of Distance
Sometimes, the only way to really understand your own world is to step outside of it. For a lot of people, crossing the Atlantic wasn’t just about geography—it felt like a leap into the unknown. It was a chance to challenge everything you thought you knew, and see old beliefs through a totally new lens.
Imagine arriving in Paris for the first time. The city is buzzing, but suddenly, you feel both thrilled and completely out of place. The language sounds different, the daily routines are unfamiliar, and even the pace of life throws you off. But in that sense of strangeness, there’s a unique kind of freedom. You get to watch, to question, and to see everything with fresh eyes. Suddenly, museums and cathedrals aren’t just historic sites—they become living classrooms. And the past? It isn’t just something you read about. It’s alive, woven into every street and building around you.
Picture this: one evening, you’re sitting in a smoky Parisian café, listening as artists and writers throw around big ideas about progress. Their debates are intense, sometimes even heated, but there’s always a spark—an energy that anything is possible. You start to realize that no country is simply old or new, or stuck between tradition and innovation. Instead, every society is wrestling with how to honor its memories while still embracing change.
That distance from home gives you a whole new perspective. Suddenly, the issues that felt so overwhelming back home—political drama, social worries—they seem a little different from far away. You start to see that every culture, every country, is dealing with its own version of uncertainty. And there’s a comfort in that. Maybe, just maybe, no one really has all the answers.
Of course, the lessons you learn in Europe aren’t always easy. There are moments when you feel lonely, frustrated, maybe even lost. But alongside the challenges, something else grows—a sense of possibility. The world turns out to be bigger, more complicated, and more beautiful than any single tradition could ever show you. Living abroad, you start to see yourself more clearly, noticing both the strengths and the blind spots of your own upbringing.
Over time, the journey stops being about running away. It becomes about returning—coming home with more than just memories. You bring back a new way of seeing the world, and a realization that education isn’t a destination. It’s a lifelong adventure—a process of discovery that never really ends.
